newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - Arbs ride to North Sea rescue.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - Arbs ride to North Sea rescue.

text.p: The opportunity to substitute for West African barrels in the U.S. Gulf refining belt may give the North Sea crude market another jolt higher this week, traders said on Monday.
The demand gap left by the flow of millions of barrels of West African grades to Asia could prove to be a much needed outlet for a North Sea market suffering from lacklustre local buying interest.
"There are very few refineries in Europe that are taking Brent, the only players on Dated Brent are trading houses," said one North Sea trader last week.
Demand for other grades was equally limp, after the usual scramble for cargoes on the release of the monthly loading programmes failed to materialise.
But a jump in Brent CFDs on Friday revealed expectations that arbitrage sales would lift the physical market this week.

Contracts for Difference (CFDs) for this week leapt by around 15 cents to June Brent -45 cents, while good buying interest for wet barrels was seen on Friday at May Brent -40 cents -- 15 cents above the last deal done.
Four of five Brents turning wet on Friday were kept by Shell, giving the market another shot in the arm.
"There is going to be some demand in the U.S. which won't be covered by delivered West African barrels," a trader said.

North Sea sellers have struggled to place barrels into the U.S. in recent weeks, but a May Dated Brent/West Texas Intermediate spread of around $2.00 a barrel on Friday set the scene for some busy trans-Atlantic traffic, said dealers.
U.S. prices have been buoyed by surge in heating oil demand caused by a late spring cold snap in the Northeastern states.
"We've not seen a lot of buying yet in Europe but refinery margins are good and the arbitrages look workable," said a trader for a European major.
"We are looking at what we can work into the U.S. Gulf and even other areas, like the Mediterranean."

Shipping broker reports of China's Sinochem fixing a VLCC to take Brent from Sullom Voe to the Croatian refinery of Rijeka, with which it has a processing arrangement, also helped boost sentiment on Friday.
West African grades are expected to extend last week's 10-15 cents gains in spot differentials as Asian buying gathers pace.
"Interest in the Far East -- Japan, Korea, Singapore and China -- is picking up for West African grades," a trader said.
"Hopefully this upbeat mood will continue into next week."
Japanese, South Korean and Chinese buyers were all active last week, picking up at least seven million barrels of Nigerian and Angolan crudes in May.
And with Singapore refining margins continuing strong, and well ahead of returns in other centres like Rotterdam and the U.S. Gulf, traders expect the buying spree to continue.

Mediterranean markets would remain focused on term price negotiations for Algerian and Syrian crudes in May but traders expect Russian Urals to soften as the week progresses. Cheaper Iraqi Kirkuk in May would keep up the pressure on the benchmark sour, traders said.
